title: Families and release models
summary: Debian, Red Hat, SUSE, Arch and Alpine families, and LTS, point and rolling releases.

steps.title: The family tree
body: Most distros descend from a few roots. Learn the roots and you know the tools for the whole branch:
| **Debian** | Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, Pop!_OS, Raspberry Pi OS, Kali | `.deb`, `apt` / `dpkg` |
| **Red Hat** | RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, Amazon Linux | `.rpm`, `dnf` (older: `yum`) / `rpm` |
Fedora is upstream of CentOS Stream, which is upstream of RHEL; Rocky and Alma rebuild RHEL-compatible releases. Amazon Linux 2023 is based on Fedora.

steps.prompt: Match the distro to its package tool.

steps.title: Release models
body: | **LTS / point release** | a numbered release every 1-3 years; versions frozen; security fixes backported for 5-10 years; minor point releases (`12.7`, `9.4`) roll up fixes | Ubuntu LTS (`24.04`, every two years, 5 years standard + more with Pro), Debian stable, RHEL, Rocky, Alma, SLES |
| **Regular (short-lived)** | a release every ~6 months, supported for about a year | Fedora, Ubuntu interim releases (`24.10`) |
| **Rolling** | no versions: you update continuously and always have the latest | Arch, openSUSE Tumbleweed, Alpine `edge`, Gentoo |
| **Stream** | a rolling preview of the next point release | CentOS Stream |
Ubuntu version numbers are the year and month: `24.04` is April 2024. Even years with `.04` are LTS.

steps.prompt: You run a payroll server that must keep working for 5 years with minimal changes. Which release model fits?
options: LTS: frozen versions with backported security fixes
steps.explain: Rolling releases change behaviour under you; 6-month releases force an upgrade every year.

steps.prompt: What does this print? (Ubuntu LTS releases are the `.04` releases of even years.)

steps.title: Is it LTS?
prompt: Write `bool IsUbuntuLts(string version)`: `true` for versions like `24.04` or `22.04.5` (an even year, month `04`), `false` otherwise (`23.04`, `24.10`, or anything that does not start with two numbers separated by a dot).

Then write `int SupportEnds(string version)` returning the year standard support ends: LTS → release year + 5, other valid releases → the year of the release plus 1 (9 months, rounded up to the next year). Use the full year: `24.04` → 2029. Return -1 for an invalid version.
solution: bool TryParse(string version, out int year, out int month)
return parts.Length >= 2 && int.TryParse(parts[0], out year) && int.TryParse(parts[1], out month);
TryParse(version, out var y, out var m) && m == 4 && y % 2 == 0;
if (!TryParse(version, out var y, out _)) return -1;
hints: Split on `.` and `int.TryParse` the first two parts.
LTS: month 4 and an even year.
